The paper does not compare methods on exactly the same layer-wise configurations. Hypervolume is additionally computed from roughly 50 CoA-LoRA points but only five reported QLoRA/LQ-LoRA bit settings, systematically favoring the more densely sampled frontier.

The claim of adaptation to arbitrary configurations is not established. The unseen-configuration sampling procedure, sample count, and distance from training configurations are omitted, and deployment selects configurations specifically constrained to be near the final training set. Quantization, per-layer SVD construction, and configuration selection are still required for a new setting, but their latency and memory costs are not reported. There are also no measurements on edge hardware, so the on-the-fly deployment claim is unsupported.

Statistical evidence is weak: no repeated runs, variance, or confidence intervals are reported. Table C.3 claims eight downstream tasks but contains seven, and every accuracy is a multiple of 0.78125, strongly suggesting evaluation on only 128 examples per task; this sample size is not disclosed and makes the small average gains unreliable.

Reproducibility is inadequate. The implementation link is incomplete, while dataset subset sizes, token counts, batch sizes, optimizer details, hardware, random seeds, finite-difference iteration count, GP/kernel settings, segment construction, baseline training parity, and complete cost accounting are missing. The hypervolume appendix also reuses f2 for task performance after defining it as average bit-width and never specifies normalization of the bit-width objective.

These issues affect the central technical and empirical claims rather than being minor presentation defects. The underlying idea is promising, but the present manuscript does not provide sufficiently sound or controlled evidence for acceptance at a top-tier venue.
